Six are national permissions to tax electricity sold to ships at a reduced rate, granted to Denmark, France, Italy, Spain, Sweden and Germany. The Spanish one reads: Spain is authorised to apply a reduced taxation rate to electricity directly supplied to vessels, other than private pleasure craft, berthed in ports, provided that the minimum levels of taxation referred to in Article 10(1) of Directive 2003/96/EC are respected. Beside them sit the EU rules on charging and fuelling points, which set binding national targets for ports and other sites (The regulation sets mandatory national targets for road vehicles, vessels and stationary aircraft), and Norway's rule for its heritage fjords, under which passenger ships shall use shore power where it is available. Set aside as background: the EU energy tax law itself and a later amendment to it, and one electricity market outlook that says nothing about ships. Two road-fuel tax reliefs are used only as edge cases under Regulations.","meaning":"For a freight operator with no sustainability background: a ship at berth normally burns its own fuel to make the power it needs there. Plugging into the port grid instead is called shore power. The rule-makers say why they want it: The use of shore-side electricity avoids emissions from burning bunker fuels at berth and contributes to an improvement in the local air quality in port cities and to noise reduction. Several governments have asked the EU for permission to tax electricity sold to ships below the normal rate. Spain's decision gives the reason for its fixed term: The authorisation is granted for a four-year period so as not to discourage relevant economic operators from making the necessary investments. Italy's decision gives its own purpose: In order to enable port and ship operators, as well as distributors and redistributors of electricity, to continue promoting the use of shore-side electricity, it is appropriate to authorise Italy to apply a reduced rate of taxation to shore-side electricity.

*Analytical inference:* each permission is national and dated, so the tax on quay-side power for a ship can differ by country and can change when a permission ends; the records do not state the tax rate any country actually applies, so the size of any saving is not known here. Binding duties come from elsewhere: inland ports must offer a connection (see Watch), and passenger ships in Norway's heritage fjords must plug in where a connection exists.","ramifications":"### Regulations
The tax permissions are temporary and individual. Denmark's decision (Done at Luxembourg, 19 June 2015) says It shall expire six years thereafter, and that should the Council, acting on the basis of Article 113 TFEU, provide for general rules on tax advantages for shore-side electricity, this Decision shall expire on the day on which those general rules become applicable.

*Analytical inference:* counted from its 2015 notification, the Danish permission ran out around 2021; no record here shows a renewal.

A non-binding Commission recommendation asked for the connections before any targets: Member States should consider the installation of shore-side electricity for use by ships at berth in ports; particularly in ports where air quality limit values are exceeded. Norway's fjord rule is wider than plugging in; it sets zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords, effective from 1 January 2026 for ships < 10,000 GT and from 1 January 2032 for ships ≥ 10,000 GT. Norway has paid for at least one: The Norwegian Government has allocated NOK 100 million to Aurland Port Authority for shore power infrastructure in Flåm, administered by Enova.

Two road-fuel reliefs sit at the edge of this theme. Sweden's falls under the current energy tax law: Sweden is authorised to apply a reduction of the rates up to 2,4 SEK per litre below the minimum levels of taxation referred to in Article 7 of Directive 2003/96/EC for gas oil and unleaded petrol used as motor fuels, because the application of a reduced rate of excise duty aims to alleviate the social and economic impacts of high retail prices of petrol and diesel resulting from the geopolitical situation and directly affecting both households and companies. A Dutch relief for taxis fell under the law that came before it: In accordance with Article 8(4) of Directive 92/81/EEC, the Netherlands is authorised to apply a degressive differentiated rate of excise duty, not exceeding NLG 0,14 per litre, on diesel fuel consumed by taxis in the period 1 January to 31 December 2000.

*Operational implication:* a forwarder who books port calls or barge moves in these countries can ask carriers whether shore power is used at berth and whether the reduced tax is passed on; the records state the permission, not the carrier's practice.

### Research
The one research record is an electricity market outlook, not a study of ships. Its one price outlook is for households in the United States: residential electricity prices are expected to increase by 5% in 2026. That is not the price a European port charges a ship, and no record here gives that price or links the outlook to ships.","watch":"- Sweden's road-fuel tax cut ends first: This Decision shall apply from 1 July 2026 until 30 November 2026. An extension would appear on Regulations as a new Council decision.
- France's shore-power permission is the next to run out: shall apply from 1 January 2021 until 31 December 2026. A renewal would appear on Regulations as a new Council implementing decision addressed to France.
- The EU charging and fuelling rules have their first review: By 31 December 2026 and every five years thereafter, the Commission shall review this Regulation. The review also looks at whether more vessels are covered, because the review assesses a possible extension of the scope of the Regulation to other ship types. The review report would appear on Regulations.
- Italy's and Sweden's shore-power permissions end next (Italy: This Decision shall apply from 1 January 2022 until 31 December 2027; Sweden: shall apply from 1 January 2024 until 31 December 2027), Spain's a year later (This Decision shall apply from 1 January 2025 until 31 December 2028) and Germany's after that (This Decision shall apply from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2029).
- Inland ports face a supply deadline: at least one installation providing shore-side electricity supply to inland waterway vessels is deployed at all TEN-T comprehensive inland waterway ports by 31 December 2029.
- Norway's zero-emission requirement for the fjords extends to the largest passenger ships: From 1 January 2032 , the same requirement will extend to ships of 10,000 GT and above. No record says whether the plug-in duty changes with it.
The next link that would change this theme most is a price: a published price for electricity supplied at berth would appear on Market Intel.","gaps":"In practice this theme is about rules only. Its records describe one cost line: what airlines pay in Europe for the carbon their fuel emits, and the cleaner jet fuel that would lower it. For airlines the free permits are gone: From 2026 onward: Full auctioning. No free allowances. Airlines must purchase all allowances at auction or on secondary markets. Fuel suppliers at EU airports must also blend cleaner fuel into jet fuel, and market records price that fuel. Research records say how far new fuels and aircraft can go; the one operations record is a UK profile that says nothing about aviation. Set aside as outside this cost line: the UN development goals, a buyers' climate coalition, three older EU decisions on the global airline offsetting scheme, and three research pages on transport in general, Latin America and Southeast Asia.","meaning":"For a freight operator with no sustainability background: the EU issues a limited number of permits to emit carbon dioxide, and EU ETS aviation obligations fall on aircraft operators. Since this year airlines buy every permit they need, and the source says what follows: The phase-out (25% reduction in 2024, 50% in 2025, full auctioning from 2026) increases the carbon cost airlines must recover through pricing on intra-EEA routes. The cost reaches a forwarder through the airline's price.

The second cost is the fuel itself. The EU blending rule reads: ReFuelEU Aviation (Regulation (EU) 2023/2405) requires aviation fuel suppliers at EU airports to blend minimum SAF levels starting at 2% from 2025, rising to 6% by 2030, 20% by 2035, 34% by 2040, 42% by 2045, and 70% by 2050. Fuel suppliers are the regulated entities. That cleaner fuel is dearer. The airline association puts it this way: SAF prices exceed fossil-based jet fuel by a factor of two, and by up to a factor of five in mandated markets; a clean-transport research council gives a wider range, a cost premium of 2.1 to 10.6 times fossil jet. One airline association record puts the European cause plainly: In Europe, ReFuelEU Aviation has sharply increased costs amid limited SAF capacity and oligopolistic supply chains. It also states that airlines paid a premium of USD 2.9 billion for the limited 1.9 Mt of SAF available in 2025. Of this, USD 1.4 billion reflects the standard SAF price premium over conventional fuel.

*Analytical inference:* an air freight rate on routes inside Europe now carries two climate costs, the permits the airline buys and the blended fuel its supplier must provide; no record here states how an airline passes either into a cargo rate or surcharge, so neither can be checked against a quote from these records alone.","ramifications":"### Regulations
For air the permit scope is still Europe-only: The EU decided to temporarily limit the scope of the EU ETS to flights within the EEA. The blending rule tightens with a share reserved for synthetic fuel: rising to 6% in 2030 including a 1.2% sub-quota for synthetic fuels. There is no carve-out for aid shipments: The Fit for 55 package does not provide a regulatory exemption from SAF costs for humanitarian cargo.

### Market Intel
Supply is the constraint: SAF production in 2025 represents only 0.6% of total jet fuel consumption, increasing to 0.8% the following year. The rules pay part of the gap; the E-Fuel Alliance says EU ETS SAF allowances (20 million, 2024–2030) are available to airlines as a cost-offset mechanism for the SAF premium — but only for intra-EU flights. Air cargo prices rose this spring (Xeneta: global air cargo spot rates rose 41% year-on-year in May to an average of $3.40 per kg); the same record notes that severe disruption at major Gulf hubs due to the war in the Middle East continued to constrain capacity on key corridors. No record attributes any of that rise to permits or fuel blending.

### Operations
The only operations record is a UK profile, and its climate rows concern ships and road, for example: The UK's 2025 Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy targets 30% GHG reduction by 2030, 80% by 2040, and zero by 2050. Nothing here describes airport, airline or air cargo operations, so this page carries no air freight fact for the theme.

### Research
For aircraft: Near zero-carbon aircraft that can undertake transatlantic flights will unlikely be widely available until the 2040s. For the fuel: The SAF commercialisation timeline will depend on reducing the cost of production, increasing efficiencies, as well as connecting components into a system that can operate effectively to deliver SAFs at scale.

*Analytical inference:* with new aircraft for long routes not expected before the 2040s, the price gap between cleaner and fossil jet fuel is where the near-term cost of the change sits for air freight.","watch":"- The EU's check on the global airline offsetting scheme was due before this brief (By July 2026, the Commission will carry out an assessment of CORSIA to determine if it is sufficiently delivering on the goals of the Paris Agreement); no record here gives its result. The law sets out what follows a negative finding: If CORSIA is assessed as inadequate, the Commission will make a legislative proposal to extend EU ETS scope to departing international flights from EEA airports (incoming flights would be exempted). A proposal would appear on Regulations.
- Brazil starts its own clean-fuel obligation for domestic flights: 1 January 2027: First SAF GHG reduction obligation for domestic air operators: 1% minimum reduction vs fossil baseline.
- Supply growth slows: in 2026, SAF production growth is projected to slow down and reach 2.4 Mt. A production figure for this year would appear on Market Intel.
- Airline targets are under pressure: the airline association says many airlines that have committed to use 10% SAF by 2030 will be forced to reevaluate these commitments. Revised airline commitments would appear on Market Intel.
